EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – Illinois Child‐Protection Investigations

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) using “caseworker removal propensity’’ (leniency/strictness) as an instrument for whether the child is placed in foster care.

Why IV is appropriate
• Treatment is a one-time, endogenous decision that is not repeatable, so panel-based DiD/Event Study logic does not apply.  
• Investigations are quasi-randomly assigned to front-line case managers whose propensity to remove varies sharply but is plausibly unrelated to any single child’s latent outcomes once we condition on rich case covariates.  
• The institutional setting is analogous to “judge leniency’’ designs that have proved powerful in criminal justice, health care, and education.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if the child was removed from the home and formally placed in foster care within 30 days of the index investigation; 0 otherwise.

Instrument  
Z_i = Leave-one-out removal rate of the assigned caseworker during the same fiscal year:  
 Z_i = (∑_{j≠i} T_j ) / ( N_{cw,fy} – 1 )

Control (counterfactual)  
Children investigated for abuse/neglect who are left at home (T_i = 0).  
Because we use an IV, the comparison of interest is between compliers—children whose placement status is changed when they are randomly assigned to a “strict’’ versus “lenient’’ caseworker.

Timing  
Event date = day the abuse/neglect investigation is opened. Outcomes are measured many years later, so there is no additional timing dimension in the research design.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Caseworker leniency strongly predicts foster-care placement.  
 Plausibility: Historical data show large cross-worker dispersion (e.g., 5th–95th percentiles of removal rates: 5 % vs. 55 %). First-stage F-statistic > 10 is expected.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on rich covariates and office-year FE, caseworker leniency affects long-run child outcomes only through the placement decision.  
 Plausibility: Caseworkers have no authority over other public programs (e.g., schooling, courts) once the investigation is closed. They rarely interact with the child after removal/no-removal decision.

A3. Random (or as-good-as-random) Assignment: Children are assigned to caseworkers quasi-randomly within office-date cells once we condition on allegation type, reporter, etc.  
 Plausibility: Centralized call center allocates cases to the “next available’’ investigator. We will validate by testing balance on pre-determined covariates across above- vs. below-median-leniency workers.

A4. Monotonicity: No child is less likely to be placed in foster care when handled by a stricter (higher-propensity) caseworker.  
 Plausibility: Unlikely that a strict investigator ever causes a removal‐prone family to remain at home (defiers). 

A5. SUTVA: One child’s assignment to foster care does not affect another child’s delinquency, fertility, or earnings.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable given large population, but we will cluster at the family level to account for any intra-household spillovers.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Non-random sorting of cases to lenient vs. strict caseworkers (violates A3).  
 Mitigation:  
 • Include detailed allegation, reporter, child demographics, month × office FE, and backlog controls.  
 • Run balance and placebo tests on pre-investigation outcomes (e.g., prior delinquency petitions for older siblings).  
 • Estimate McCrary-type density tests of covariates on instrument.

Threat 2: Caseworker leniency may correlate with unobserved service quality (violates A2).  
 Mitigation:  
 • Restrict sample to investigators whose employment spells are short and non-overlapping with service-delivery staff.  
 • Include office × year FE; within-office variation eliminates correlated resource shocks.  
 • Test whether leniency predicts service utilization among the children who are NOT removed (should be zero).

Threat 3: Weak instrument for sub-samples (e.g., teen motherhood sample).  
 Mitigation:  
 • Report first-stage F-statistics for every outcome sample.  
 • Collapse to larger “director-level’’ propensity instrument if needed.  
 • Use LIML and Anderson–Rubin confidence sets as robustness.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data work
library(fixest)       # IV regression with high-D FE
library(modelsummary) # pretty tables

# 1. Load & Merge --------------------------------------------------------
d  <- fread("illinois_abuse_investigations.csv")        # child-level file
cw <- fread("caseworker_characteristics.csv")           # one row per cw-year
d  <- merge(d, cw, by = c("caseworker_id","fiscal_year"), all.x = TRUE)

# 2. Variable Construction ----------------------------------------------
# treatment: removal within 30 days
d[, placed := as.integer(days_to_removal <= 30)]

# instrument: leave-one-out removal rate of cw in fiscal year
d[, cw_n   := .N, by = .(caseworker_id, fiscal_year)]
d[, cw_sum := sum(placed), by = .(caseworker_id, fiscal_year)]
d[, leniency := (cw_sum - placed)/(cw_n - 1)]           # leave-one-out
d[leniency < 0, leniency := NA]                         # single-case workers

# main outcomes
d[, delinquency := as.integer(num_juvenile_petitions > 0)]
d[, teen_mom    := as.integer(teen_birth == 1 & sex == "F")]
d[, work_frac   := qtrs_worked/elig_qtrs]
d[, earnings    := avg_qtr_earn]

# 3. Controls ------------------------------------------------------------
controls <- ~ factor(reporter) + factor(allegation) + factor(race_eth) +
             sex + factor(age_at_report) + factor(month) + 
             factor(fiscal_year) + factor(cook_county)

# 4. 2SLS – Example: juvenile delinquency sample -------------------------
delin_sample <- d[!is.na(delinquency)]

iv_delin <- feols(delinquency ~ 1 | placed ~ leniency | 0 | caseworker_id,
                  data = delin_sample,
                  split = TRUE, # speed
                  cluster = ~caseworker_id + family_id,  # multiway cluster
                  fixef = ~ office_id^fiscal_year,       # office × year FE
                  add_f  = controls)

etable(iv_delin, keep = "placed", se.below = TRUE)

# 5. Robustness: alternative instrument (office-year leniency) ----------
d[, off_n   := .N, by = .(office_id, fiscal_year)]
d[, off_sum := sum(placed), by = .(office_id, fiscal_year)]
d[, off_len := (off_sum - placed)/(off_n - 1)]

iv_alt <- feols(delinquency ~ 1 | placed ~ off_len | 0 | office_id,
                data = delin_sample, cluster = ~office_id, add_f = controls)

etable(iv_alt, keep = "placed", se.below = TRUE)
```

(Replicate code for teen motherhood, work fraction, and earnings; switch outcome on left side.)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior from economic theory and existing qualitative work suggests removal may disrupt peer environment and schooling but also removes children from abusive homes.

• Juvenile delinquency: I expect a modest *increase* (5–8 pp) among compliers because instability and separation from kin raise antisocial behavior.  
• Teen motherhood: Ambiguous; if removal places girls with stricter supervision, teen birth could fall. Predict a −4 pp effect.  
• Employment & earnings (ages 20–30): Probably negative (≈ −0.05 SD in work fraction; −$500 / quarter) due to educational disruption.

Magnitude is, of course, an empirical question; these are informed priors.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument strongly predicts treatment (relevance)…………………………1  
C2: Instrument excludable after controls (exclusion)……………………………0.5  
C3: Random assignment / no sorting (independence)……………………………0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers)………………………………………………………………1  
C5: SUTVA & no interference………………………………………………………………0.5  

Overall: 3.5 / 5 – respectable but requires careful balance and placebo tests.
